drills.title: DPI, RVPI, TVPI
drills.question: A fund has called $80m, distributed $24m and reports NAV of $76m. Give DPI, RVPI and TVPI.
drills.solution: DPI = 24/80 = 0.30x. RVPI = 76/80 = 0.95x. TVPI = 1.25x, of which 76% is an estimate.
common_mistakes: Dividing by commitments instead of paid-in capital
Reporting TVPI as if it were realized
drills.intuition: Only DPI is cash. RVPI is the GP's estimate of what is left.
drills.takeaway: Early in a fund's life, TVPI is mostly an appraisal.

drills.title: Auction round trip
drills.question: A work is bought at an $800,000 hammer with a 27% buyer's premium and later resold at the same hammer with a 10% seller's commission. What is the round-trip cost, and the annual drag over a 5-year hold?
common_mistakes: Ignoring the premium because an index measures hammer prices
drills.intuition: Two fees on two different bases: the premium is on top of the hammer, the commission comes out of it.
drills.takeaway: Hammer prices must rise about 6.7% a year for five years just to get the money back.

drills.title: TVPI versus KS-PME
drills.question: Calls of 50 at years 0 and 1, distributions of 60 at year 2 and 90 at year 3. Index levels 100, 120, 140, 150. Compute TVPI and KS-PME. Did the fund beat the index?

rubric: Computes TVPI = 150/100 = 1.50x
Interprets KS-PME > 1 as outperformance in index units, not risk-adjusted
Notes that a 1.50x multiple overstates the advantage because the index itself rose 50%
Asks about the fund's leverage (beta above one) before calling it skill

drills.solution: TVPI = 1.50x. Index units: calls 0.5 + 0.4167 = 0.9167; distributions 0.4286 + 0.6 = 1.0286. KS-PME = 1.12. The fund beat the index by 12% in index units over three years, before any beta adjustment.
common_mistakes: Comparing TVPI with the index's 1.50x end level and concluding the fund merely matched
Discounting at a fixed rate instead of the realized index return
drills.intuition: KS-PME converts every dollar into index units on its own date.
drills.takeaway: Report a PME with every private-fund multiple.

drills.title: A discount to a stale NAV
drills.question: A seller offers an LP interest at 82% of a $40.0m NAV struck before listed comparables fell 18%. The fund's beta to that index is about 1.4. A colleague says it is an 18% discount. Re-mark the NAV and state the bid against it. Would you buy?

rubric: Computes corrected value 40 x (1 - 1.4 x 0.18) = 29.92
Computes 32.8/29.92 - 1 = +9.6%: a premium, not a discount
Questions the beta estimate and tests a second value
Considers unfunded commitments and the remaining J-curve
Declines at this price or re-bids below corrected NAV; states what would change the view (an updated mark, portfolio detail)

drills.solution: Corrected NAV = 40.0 x (1 - 0.252) = $29.92m. Bid = 0.82 x 40 = $32.8m, 9.6% above corrected value. Re-bid below about $29.9m less a liquidity discount, or wait for the next mark.
common_mistakes: Accepting the stale mark as current value
Ignoring unfunded commitments that come with the interest
drills.intuition: A discount to an old price can be a premium to the current one.

drills.title: The fund without the unicorn
drills.question: Seed deals have a mean multiple of 2.4x; 3% of deals return 40x. A manager makes 15 independent equal-sized investments. What is the probability the fund holds no 40x deal, and its expected multiple in that case? What should an LP expect from one commitment?

rubric: Concludes the median commitment is far below the 2.4x mean
Links the result to portfolio size and to manager access
Sizes the commitment so that a sub-1.5x outcome is acceptable

drills.solution: P(no 40x) = 0.97^15 = 63.3%. Conditional mean = 1.2/0.97 = 1.24x. Most single commitments will not contain the deal that makes the average.
common_mistakes: Treating the mean as the typical outcome
Assuming diversification raises the mean (it raises the median)
drills.intuition: Half the average comes from 3% of deals.
drills.takeaway: Underwrite venture commitments on the median, not the mean.

drills.title: Collateral the borrower printed

inputs.collateral: borrower's affiliated exchange token, market value $90m

drills.question: A trading firm asks the family office for a $50m one-year loan at 14%, secured by $90m (180% coverage) of a token issued by its affiliated exchange. Daily token volume is about $12m. The firm's financials are unaudited, the firm's CEO says the token 'cannot fall below $20 because we will buy it', and a broker says three other lenders have already committed. Information on who else holds the token is not available. Decide.

rubric: Identifies the collateral as self-referential: its value falls when the borrower's solvency is questioned
Notes that $90m of collateral is 7.5 days of total market volume, so liquidation value is far below market value
Treats the price-support promise as a liability of the same borrower, not as protection
Treats other lenders' commitments as non-evidence (and possibly as competing claims on the same collateral)
Recommends abstention, or states conditions (independent collateral, audited accounts) so strict they amount to abstention

drills.solution: Abstain. Haircut the token to near zero in the stress state, because it is most likely to collapse when the borrower defaults. Coverage of 180% at market is close to 0% in the state that matters. 14% does not compensate for an unsecured loan to an unaudited borrower. This is the structure documented in the 2022 FTX/Alameda episode (Chapter 19 §19.9).
common_mistakes: Treating a liquid quoted price as liquidation value
drills.intuition: Collateral is only valuable if it is worth something when the borrower is not.
drills.takeaway: Self-issued collateral is unsecured credit with extra steps.
